source_text: Plane monet Romanos omnibus potestatibus subjici, quia non sit potestas nisi a Deo, quia non sine caussa gladium gestet, et quia ministerium sit Dei; sed et ultrix, inquit, in iram ei qui malum fecerit. Nam et praemiserat: Principes enim non sunt timori bono operi, sed malo. Vis autem non timere potestatem? fac bonum, et laudem ab ea referes. Dei ergo ministra est tibi in bonum. Si vero malum facias, time. Ita, non in occasione frustrandi martyrii jubet te subjici potestatibus, sed in provocatione bene vivendi, etiam sub illarum respectu, quasi adjutricum justitiae, quasi ministrarum divini judicii, hic etiam de nocentibus praejudicantis. Dehinc et exequitur quomodo velit te subjici potestatibus, reddere jubens, cui tributum, tributum; cui vectigal, vectigal; id est quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari, et quae Dei, Deo; solius autem Dei homo. Condixerat scilicet Petrus, regem quidem honorandum; ut tamen tunc rex honoretur, cum suis rebus insistit, cum a divinis honoribus longe est; quia et pater et mater diligentur, cum Deo non comparabuntur. Caeterum, super Deum diligi nec animam licebit.
pass_a_gloss: It clearly warns the Romans to be subject to all powers, because there is no power except from God, because he does not bear the sword without cause, and because it is a ministry of God; but also avenging, it says, in wrath to him who has done evil. For it had previously said: For rulers are not a terror to good work, but to evil. Do you want not to fear power? Do good, and you will receive praise from it. Therefore, it is a minister of God to you for good. But if you do evil, fear. Thus, it does not command you to be subject to powers on the occasion of frustrating martyrdom, but in the provocation of living well, even under their regard, as if a helper of justice, as if a minister of divine judgment, here also prejudging concerning those who do harm. Next, it also follows how it wants you to be subject to powers, commanding to render to him who is due tribute, tribute; to him who is due tax, tax; that is, the things that are Caesar's, to Caesar, and the things that are God's, to God; but man is God's alone. Certainly, Peter had agreed that a king is to be honored; yet the king is to be honored only when he stands by his own things, when he is far from divine honors; because also a father and a mother are loved, when they are not compared to God. Moreover, it will not be permitted to love anything more than God, not even the soul.

choices.why: feminine form of ultrix, meaning avenging or punishing
referring to the role of authorities as servants of God
emphasizing that humans belong to God alone

choices.english: it will not be permitted to love anything more than God, not even the soul
rejected: love God more than your soul
choices.why: correct translation of the Latin phrase

bible_refs.note: reference to rendering to Caesar what is Caesar's

pass_b_english: Tertullian bluntly warns the Romans to submit to every governing authority, since no power exists except by God's decree, the sword is not borne without reason, and the ruler serves as God's minister (Romans 13:1-7). Yet that ministry has teeth: the ruler is also an avenger who executes wrath on the evildoer. After all, Scripture had already said rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil. Do you want to live without fear of authority? Then do what is right, and you will win its approval. So the ruler is God's servant for your benefit. But if you do wrong, be afraid. Therefore, this command to submit is not given to frustrate martyrdom, but to provoke upright living even under the rulers' gaze, treating them as allies of justice and ministers of divine judgment who even now pass preliminary sentence on wrongdoers. Next Paul spells out what that submission looks like: pay what is owed — tribute to whom tribute is due, tax to whom tax is due (Romans 13:7). In other words, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's (Matthew 22:21); the human being belongs to God alone. Peter, too, had agreed that the king deserves honor — but only when the king stays in his lane, keeping his distance from divine honors, just as father and mother are loved precisely when they are not equated with God. Beyond that, nothing — not even one's own soul — may be loved above God.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass B correctly identifies the implied scriptural context (Romans 13 and Matthew 22) which are alluded to in the Latin text, providing the required inline citations. The distinction in the final sentence regarding the soul and God is preserved. All clauses in the Latin are accounted for in both Pass A and B.
